children: , the largest U.S. bank by assets, raised its prime lending rate to 7% from 6.75% after the Federal Reserve's quarter-point rate increase. JPMorgan shares slipped approximately 0.2% to $348.29 Thursday morning.

The prime rate is a key benchmark for borrowing costs across products such as credit cards and personal loans. Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and several regional lenders made similar moves. But the math is not automatic: loans and deposits reset at different speeds, so a 25-basis-point increase in the prime rate does not mean JPMorgan captures a matching boost in lending margins.

That tension is what investors need to watch. Higher loan yields can lift net interest income when deposit costs move more slowly, but tighter rates can also cool borrowing, squeeze customers with variable-rate debt and eventually weigh on credit quality. The chart adds another valuation wrinkle: JPMorgan's $348.29 share price sits 9.7% above its $317.50 GF Value, suggesting the market is already pricing in a meaningful amount of strength.

title: JPMorgan Falls as Prime Lending Reprices to 7%
